resources.title: 📘 1 · Notes: Elbow & Forearm (Full) — 200L Anatomy
resources.content: > How to use this page: Read top to bottom once, then do the 60-second box, the exam points, and the flashcards. Bloom's levels are shown as \[R\] Recall, \[U\] Understand, \[A\] Apply, \[An\] Analyse. Draft built from the standard atlas order (Netter plates 426–441). Reorder to Bowen's lecture sequence once their outline is confirmed. ## 0. Study plan (suggested 3 sessions) - Session 1 \[U\]: Sections 1–3 (joints, bones, membrane). Draw the elbow joint from memory. - Session 2 \[U\]\[A\]: Sections 4–6 (compartments and nerves). Trace each nerve on the diagram. - Session 3 \[A\]\[An\]: Sections 7–9 (cubital fossa, clinical, scenarios). Then do the flashcards and quiz pages. --- ## 1. Learning outcomes - \[R\] Name every bone, joint, ligament and landmark of the elbow and forearm. - \[U\] Explain how the elbow joint moves and why the radioulnar joints allow pronation and supination. - \[U\] Group the forearm muscles into compartments and layers, and state each one's nerve supply. - \[A\] Predict the deficit that follows a nerve injury at a named site. - \[An\] Compare the cubital fossa with the anatomical snuffbox and the carpal tunnel in terms of boundaries and contents. --- ## 2. Bones and landmarks Humerus (distal end) - Capitulum: lateral, articulates with the radial head. - Trochlea: medial, articulates with the ulna (trochlear notch). - Medial epicondyle: origin of the common flexor group. The ulnar nerve runs behind it. - Lateral epicondyle: origin of the common extensor group. - Coronoid fossa (anterior) and olecranon fossa (posterior): receive the coronoid process and olecranon during flexion and extension. Radius - Head: disc-shaped, articulates with the capitulum and the radial notch of the ulna. - Neck: site of the annular ligament attachment. - Radial tuberosity: insertion of biceps brachii. - Styloid process (distal): lateral side of the wrist. - Dorsal tubercle (Lister's tubercle): groove for extensor pollicis longus. Ulna - Olecranon: the elbow point; triceps inserts here. - Coronoid process: anterior, forms the front of the trochlear notch. - Radial notch: articulates with the radial head. - Styloid process (distal): medial side of the wrist. Interosseous membrane: fibrous sheet between radius and ulna. It transmits load from hand to forearm and gives origin to deep muscles. --- ## 3. Elbow joint Structure: one capsule, three joints 1. Humeroulnar joint: hinge (trochlea and trochlear notch). Main stability joint. 2. Humeroradial joint: capitulum and radial head. Part of the hinge, allows some rotation. 3. Proximal radioulnar joint: pivot. Radial head rotates inside the annular ligament. Ligaments - Ulnar (medial) collateral: anterior, posterior and transverse bands. Resists valgus stress. Injured in throwing athletes (Tommy John surgery). - Radial (lateral) collateral: resists varus stress. - Annular ligament: encircles the radial head. Stops it from slipping out of the radial notch. - Quadrate ligament: supports the neck of the radius below the annular ligament. Movements - Flexion and extension: humeroulnar (main) and humeroradial. - Range: flexion about 140–150°, extension about 0° (full extension is the 'carrying angle' position). - Carrying angle: about 10–15° in men, slightly more in women. Angle between arm and forearm in full extension. Nerves and blood supply of the joint - Nerves: musculocutaneous, median, ulnar, radial (articular branches). - Arteries: anastomosis around the elbow (brachial, radial and ulnar recurrent, interosseous recurrent). Exam note: The elbow is a hinge joint, but the radial head makes it a compound joint. This is why fracture of the radial head can limit pronation and supination. --- ## 4. Radioulnar joints and forearm movements Proximal radioulnar joint: pivot joint. Radial head rotates inside the annular ligament. Distal radioulnar joint: pivot joint at the ulnar head and the radial ulnar notch. Separated from the wrist joint by the articular disc. Pronation and supination - Supination: palm up. Biceps brachii and supinator. Biceps is the strongest supinator in the flexed elbow. - Pronation: palm down. Pronator teres and pronator quadratus. - Range: about 80–90° each way. - Mnemonic for supinator and biceps: 'Supination is done by the biceps' (the biceps is the strongest supinator when the elbow is flexed). --- ## 5. Anterior (flexor) compartment Common flexor origin: medial epicondyle of the humerus. Superficial layer (all from common flexor origin, medial epicondyle) | Muscle | Nerve (roots) | Action | Key note | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Pronator teres | Median (C6–7) | Pronates, weakly flexes the elbow | Median nerve passes between its two heads | | Flexor carpi radialis | Median (C6–7) | Flexes and abducts the wrist | Lateral tendon, pulse site (radial artery) | | Palmaris longus | Median (C7–8) | Flexes the wrist, tenses palmar aponeurosis | Absent in about 15% of people | | Flexor carpi ulnaris | Ulnar (C8–T1) | Flexes and adducts the wrist | Ulnar head attaches to olecranon | Intermediate layer | Muscle | Nerve | Action | Key note | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS) | Median (C7–T1) | Flexes middle phalanges of digits 2–5 | Tendons pass through FDP's split | Deep layer | Muscle | Nerve | Action | Key note | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) | Medial half: ulnar. Lateral half: AIN | Flexes distal phalanges of digits 2–5 | Only muscle that flexes the distal interphalangeal joints | | Flexor pollicis longus (FPL) | AIN (C7–T1) | Flexes the thumb's distal phalanx | Lateral deep muscle | | Pronator quadratus | AIN (C8–T1) | Pronates the forearm | Deepest, square, near the wrist | Exam note: AIN supplies FPL, FDP (lateral half) and pronator quadratus. It's the only motor-only branch of the median nerve. --- ## 6. Posterior (extensor) compartment Common extensor origin: lateral epicondyle of the humerus. Superficial group | Muscle | Nerve | Action | Key note | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Extensor carpi radialis longus (ECRL) | Radial (C6–7) | Extends and abducts the wrist | Lies on the lateral side of the forearm, not posterior. Radial nerve supplies it | | Extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB) | Deep radial (PIN) | Extends and abducts the wrist | Most common site of tennis elbow | | Extensor digitorum (ED) | PIN (C7–8) | Extends digits 2–5 | Extensor expansion (hood) | | Extensor digiti minimi (EDM) | PIN (C7–8) | Extends the little finger | Often tendon of ED | | Extensor carpi ulnaris (ECU) | PIN (C7–8) | Extends and adducts the wrist | Lies on the medial side of the posterior compartment | | Anconeus | Radial (C7–8) | Extends the elbow, stabilises the joint | Small triangular muscle at the elbow | Deep group | Muscle | Nerve | Action | Key note | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Supinator | PIN (C6–7) | Supinates the forearm | The PIN passes through it (arcade of Frohse) | | Abductor pollicis longus (APL) | PIN (C7–8) | Abducts the thumb | 'Snuffbox' boundary | | Extensor pollicis brevis (EPB) | PIN (C7–8) | Extends the thumb's proximal phalanx | 'Snuffbox' boundary | | Extensor pollicis longus (EPL) | PIN (C7–8) | Extends the thumb's distal phalanx | Wraps around Lister's tubercle | | Extensor indicis (EI) | PIN (C7–8) | Extends the index finger | Lies deep to ED | Exam note: Radial nerve gives superficial branch (sensory, lateral forearm) and deep branch (= PIN, motor to posterior compartment). --- ## 7. Lateral compartment - Brachioradialis: radial nerve (C5–6). Flexes the elbow in mid-position. Forms the lateral boundary of the cubital fossa. - ECRL: see section 6. --- ## 8. Nerves: course and deficits Median nerve (C6–T1) - Course: arm (anterior to brachial artery at the elbow) → cubital fossa → between two heads of pronator teres → under arch of FDS → carpal tunnel. - Branches in forearm: to pronator teres, FCR, palmaris longus, FDS, AIN. - Deficit if injured at the wrist (carpal tunnel): loss of thenar muscles, pinch weakness, sensory loss on palmar side of digits 1–3 and half of digit 4. - Deficit if injured above the elbow: loss of pronation, wrist and finger flexion weakness, plus sensory loss. Ulnar nerve (C8–T1) - Course: behind medial epicondyle (cubital tunnel) → between two heads of FCU → distal forearm, lateral to FCU tendon → hand. - Forearm branches: to FCU and the medial half of FDP. - Deficit at the elbow: claw hand (digits 4–5), loss of finger abduction and adduction, sensory loss on medial hand. Radial nerve (C5–T1) - Course: spiral groove of the humerus → lateral intermuscular septum → between brachialis and brachioradialis → divides into superficial and deep branches at the lateral epicondyle. - Superficial branch: sensory only, dorsal lateral hand and fingers. - Deep branch (PIN): motor only to posterior compartment. Passes through supinator. - Deficit at the spiral groove: wrist drop, loss of extension of all digits and wrist, sensory loss on dorsum of hand (the classic 'wrist drop'). - Deficit at the supinator (PIN): finger drop, but the wrist can still extend (ECRL and ECRB are spared). Common in radial head fractures. Anterior interosseous nerve (AIN) - Course: branch of median nerve in the proximal forearm, runs with the anterior interosseous artery on the interosseous membrane. - Supplies: FPL, FDP (lateral half), pronator quadratus. - Deficit: 'OK sign' lost (cannot flex thumb or index fingertip). No sensory loss. --- ## 9. Arteries of the forearm - Brachial artery: divides at the cubital fossa (about level of the radial head). - Radial artery: lateral, pulse felt at the wrist, lies deep to brachioradialis and FCR. - Ulnar artery: medial, passes deep to FCU in the upper forearm, then superficial at the wrist. Lies lateral to the ulnar nerve. - Anterior interosseous artery: arises from the common trunk of the ulnar artery, runs on the interosseous membrane with the AIN. - Anastomoses around the elbow: essential for collateral circulation after brachial artery injury. --- ## 10. Cubital fossa (high-yield) - Boundaries: - Medial: pronator teres - Lateral: brachioradialis - Superior: imaginary line joining the two epicondyles - Floor: brachialis (medial) and supinator (lateral) - Roof: deep fascia and skin (superficial structures, including median cubital vein) - Contents, lateral to medial: biceps tendon, median nerve, brachial artery. Memory: B-M-A ('Biceps, Median nerve, Artery'). - Clinical use: venepuncture site (median cubital vein). Brachial artery pulse felt just medial to the biceps tendon. --- ## 11. Clinical correlations (what the exam asks) - Carpal tunnel syndrome: median nerve compression at the wrist. Thenar wasting, numbness of digits 1–3. Tinel and Phalen tests positive. - AIN syndrome: OK sign lost; no sensory loss. Often follows elbow or forearm trauma. - Wrist drop (radial nerve at spiral groove): from humeral shaft fracture or prolonged arm compression ('Saturday night palsy'). - Finger drop (PIN injury): supinator compression or radial head fracture. - Cubital tunnel syndrome: ulnar nerve compression behind medial epicondyle. Claw hand, numbness of digits 4–5. - Tennis elbow (lateral epicondylitis): overuse of ECRB origin. Pain on resisted wrist extension. - Golfer's elbow (medial epicondylitis): overuse of common flexor origin. Pain on resisted wrist flexion. - Supracondylar fracture of humerus (children): can injure the median or AIN, and the brachial artery. --- ## 12. Real-life applications - Typing and phone use: repetitive ECRB and FDS load can cause tennis-elbow-type pain. - Driving: pronation and supination with steering wheel depend on FPL and biceps. - Sports (throwing, racket sports, golf): medial and lateral epicondyle origins take the strain. - Clinic: the cubital fossa is the standard IV and blood-draw site. Know its contents before you put a needle in. - Physiotherapy: strengthening supinators and pronators after radial head fracture. --- ## 13. Mind map (text version) ```javascript ELBOW & FOREARM ├── Bones: humerus (capitulum, trochlea, epicondyles), radius, ulna, interosseous membrane ├── Elbow joint: humeroulnar (hinge), humeroradial, proximal radioulnar (pivot) │ ├── Ligaments: ulnar collateral, radial collateral, annular, quadrate │ └── Movements: flexion/extension, pronation/supination (80–90° each way) ├── Anterior compartment │ ├── Superficial (medial epicondyle): PT, FCR, PL, FCU │ ├── Intermediate: FDS │ └── Deep: FDP, FPL, PQ (AIN) ├── Posterior compartment │ ├── Superficial (lateral epicondyle): ECRL, ECRB, ED, EDM, ECU, anconeus │ └── Deep: supinator, APL, EPB, EPL, EI (PIN) ├── Nerves: median (pronator teres, carpal tunnel), ulnar (cubital tunnel), radial (spiral groove, PIN) ├── Cubital fossa: B-M-A, boundaries PT, BR, epicondyle line └── Clinical: carpal tunnel, wrist drop, claw hand, tennis elbow, golfer's elbow ``` --- ## 14. Exam points (high yield) - AIN supplies FPL, FDP (lateral half), PQ. Motor only. - Radial nerve deep branch = PIN; passes through supinator. - Cubital fossa: B-M-A, lateral to medial. - Median nerve: between two heads of pronator teres; under arch of FDS. - Ulnar nerve: behind medial epicondyle; between two heads of FCU. - Biceps is the strongest supinator when the elbow is flexed. - Wrist drop = radial nerve (spiral groove). Finger drop (wrist extension preserved) = PIN. - Claw hand (digits 4–5) = ulnar nerve. - 'OK sign' loss = AIN. - Palmaris longus absent in about 15%. --- ## 15. Lecture takeaways (60-second box) 1. The elbow is one capsule, three joints. 2. Forearm muscles: flexors from the medial epicondyle, extensors from the lateral epicondyle. 3. Three nerves, three classic deficits: median (hand), ulnar (claw), radial (wrist drop). 4. Cubital fossa: B-M-A. 5. The AIN is motor only: OK sign. --- ## 16. Clinical scenarios (answers on the 'Scenarios & Vignettes' page) - Scenario A: A 28-year-old cyclist falls on an outstretched hand and cannot extend his wrist or fingers at the metacarpophalangeal joints. Which nerve is most likely injured, and where? - Scenario B: A 45-year-old office worker has pain on the outer part of the elbow when lifting a cup. Which muscle origin is affected? - Scenario C: A nurse notices that a patient cannot make an 'OK sign' after a forearm laceration. What is the injury, and what is spared? --- ## 17. Sources - Netter's Atlas of Human Anatomy, 7th ed., Section 7 (Upper Limb), plates 426–441. - BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy, Vol 1, Upper Limb chapters (cross-check attachments before exam). - Verify all content against Bowen's official course outline once confirmed.

resources.content: > How to use: Each row is one card. Front first, then flip. Rate yourself after each card in the Anki rating column (Again / Hard / Good / Easy). Repeat any card rated Again the same day. Image cards point to the diagrams: attach forearm_anterior.png and forearm_posterior.png to the notes page. ## A. Theory flashcards (Anki-style) | # | Front | Back | Bloom | Anki rating | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | T1 | How many joints are inside the elbow capsule? | Three: humeroulnar, humeroradial, proximal radioulnar | R | | | T2 | Type of humeroulnar joint? | Hinge (trochlea and trochlear notch) | R | | | T3 | Which ligament stops the radial head slipping out? | Annular ligament | R | | | T4 | Which ligament resists valgus stress at the elbow? | Ulnar (medial) collateral ligament | U | | | T5 | Range of forearm supination and pronation? | About 80–90° each way | R | | | T6 | Which muscle is the strongest supinator when the elbow is flexed? | Biceps brachii | U | | | T7 | Origin of the common flexor group? | Medial epicondyle of the humerus | R | | | T8 | Origin of the common extensor group? | Lateral epicondyle of the humerus | R | | | T9 | Nerve supply of pronator teres? | Median nerve (C6–7) | R | | | T10 | Nerve supply of flexor carpi ulnaris? | Ulnar nerve (C8–T1) | R | | | T11 | Which muscle is absent in about 15% of people? | Palmaris longus | R | | | T12 | Which flexor digitorum muscle is split to let FDP through? | Flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS) | U | | | T13 | Nerve supply of FDP (medial half)? | Ulnar nerve | R | | | T14 | Nerve supply of FDP (lateral half)? | Anterior interosseous nerve | R | | | T15 | Which flexor is the deepest muscle and pronates the forearm? | Pronator quadratus (AIN) | U | | | T16 | Which muscle is the only motor-only branch of the median nerve? | Anterior interosseous nerve (AIN) | U | | | T17 | Which nerve does the posterior interosseous nerve come from? | Deep branch of the radial nerve | U | | | T18 | Which muscle does the PIN pass through? | Supinator | R | | | T19 | Where does extensor pollicis longus wrap? | Lister's tubercle (dorsal radius) | U | | | T20 | What is the carrying angle? | Angle between arm and forearm in full extension, about 10–15° | R | | | T21 | Boundaries of the cubital fossa (medial, lateral, superior)? | Pronator teres; brachioradialis; imaginary line between epicondyles | R | | | T22 | Contents of the cubital fossa, lateral to medial? | Biceps tendon, median nerve, brachial artery (B-M-A) | R | | | T23 | Where does the brachial artery divide? | Cubital fossa (radial and ulnar arteries) | U | | | T24 | Which nerve is compressed in cubital tunnel syndrome? | Ulnar nerve, behind the medial epicondyle | U | | | T25 | Which nerve does the Tinel test check for? | Median nerve at the wrist (carpal tunnel) | A | | ## B. Image-based flashcards (identify on the diagrams) Front: the image and the label prompt. Back: the answer. | # | Front (look at the image) | Back | Image | Bloom | Anki rating | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | I1 | Top layer of the anterior forearm, first label | Superficial layer: pronator teres, FCR, palmaris longus, FCU | forearm\_anterior.png | R | | | I2 | Middle layer of the anterior forearm | Intermediate: FDS | forearm\_anterior.png | R | | | I3 | Deepest layer with the AIN supply | Deep: FDP (lateral half, AIN), FPL (AIN), pronator quadratus (AIN) | forearm\_anterior.png | U | | | I4 | Which group starts at the lateral epicondyle? | Posterior superficial extensor group: ECRL, ECRB, ED, EDM, ECU, anconeus | forearm\_posterior.png | R | | | I5 | Which muscle lies between the superficial and deep extensor groups in the posterior diagram? | Supinator (deep group, PIN passes through) | forearm\_posterior.png | U | | | I6 | Name the deep posterior muscles that form the snuffbox boundaries | APL, EPB, EPL (and EI nearby) | forearm\_posterior.png | A | | ## C. Scenario flashcards | # | Front | Back | Bloom | Anki rating | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | S1 | Patient cannot extend the wrist or fingers after a humeral shaft fracture. Which nerve and site? | Radial nerve at the spiral groove (wrist drop) | A | | | S2 | Patient can extend the wrist but not the fingers. Which nerve and site? | Posterior interosseous nerve (PIN), at the supinator | A | | | S3 | Patient has a claw hand (digits 4–5) after elbow injury. Which nerve? | Ulnar nerve, often at the cubital tunnel | A | | | S4 | Patient cannot make the OK sign after forearm laceration. What is lost? | AIN function: FPL, FDP (lateral half), pronator quadratus | A | | | S5 | Office worker has pain at the lateral elbow on wrist extension. Which origin? | Common extensor origin, lateral epicondyle (ECRB most often) | An | | | S6 | Hand numbness over palm of digits 1–3 at night, weak thumb pinch. Which nerve? | Median nerve at the carpal tunnel | An | | ## D. Anki quick rules - Again: card back in 10 minutes. - Hard: card back tomorrow. - Good: card back in 3 days. - Easy: card back in 7+ days. - Target: 20 new cards per day, 60 reviews per day. Pause new cards when reviews back up.

resources.title: ✅ 3 · Quiz: Elbow & Forearm (Objective + Essay) — 200L Anatomy
resources.content: > How to use: Answer each question before checking the key at the bottom. Bloom levels: R recall, U understand, A apply, An analyse. Essay prompts are marked with a guide. ## A. Objective questions (single best answer) | # | Question | A | B | C | D | Answer | Bloom | Why | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 1 | Which muscle is supplied by the AIN? | Flexor carpi ulnaris | Flexor pollicis longus | Palmaris longus | Extensor digitorum | B | R | FPL is an AIN muscle | | 2 | Median nerve passes between which two structures in the forearm? | Two heads of FCU | Two heads of pronator teres | Brachioradialis and biceps | Supinator and anconeus | B | U | Median nerve path | | 3 | Which is NOT a cubital fossa boundary? | Pronator teres | Brachioradialis | Brachialis | Epicondyle line | C | U | Brachialis is the floor, not a boundary | | 4 | Wrist drop follows injury to which nerve? | Ulnar | Median | Radial at spiral groove | AIN | C | A | Radial nerve, extensors | | 5 | PIN is the continuation of which nerve? | Median | Ulnar | Radial (deep branch) | Musculocutaneous | C | U | Radial deep branch | | 6 | Principal supinator of the forearm? | Biceps brachii | Supinator | Brachioradialis | Anconeus | B | R | Supinator muscle | | 7 | Muscle that flexes the middle phalanges of digits 2–5? | FDP | FDS | Palmaris longus | FCU | B | R | FDS | | 8 | Which compartment contains ECRL? | Anterior | Posterior | Lateral | Deep posterior only | C | U | ECRL is lateral | | 9 | Carpal tunnel syndrome usually causes numbness in which digits? | 1–3 | 3–5 | 4–5 only | 2 only | A | A | Median nerve sensory field | | 10 | Which elbow ligament is on the medial side? | Radial collateral | Annular | Ulnar collateral | Oblique | C | R | Ulnar collateral | | 11 | Which nerve supplies the lateral half of FDP? | Ulnar | Median | AIN | PIN | C | U | AIN | | 12 | Which nerve is injured in tennis elbow? | No nerve; overuse of ECRB origin | Ulnar | Median | AIN | A | An | Tendon overuse | | 13 | Claw hand (digits 4–5) points to which nerve? | Median | Ulnar | Radial | AIN | B | A | Ulnar intrinsic loss | | 14 | Which structure is lateral to the median nerve in the cubital fossa? | Biceps tendon | Brachial artery | Ulnar nerve | Basilic vein | A | U | B-M-A order | | 15 | Brachial artery divides into which two arteries? | Radial and ulnar | Radial and AIN | Ulnar and PIN | Radial and median | A | R | Brachial bifurcation | | 16 | Which muscle inserts on the radial tuberosity? | Biceps brachii | Brachialis | Triceps | Supinator | A | R | Biceps | | 17 | Which muscle inserts on the olecranon? | Triceps | Brachialis | Biceps | Anconeus | A | R | Triceps | | 18 | Which nerve innervates pronator quadratus? | Median | AIN | Ulnar | PIN | B | U | AIN | | 19 | Which muscle passes through the cubital tunnel? | None; the ulnar nerve passes | Pronator teres | Biceps | FCU | A | U | Ulnar nerve only | | 20 | Which joint is pivot type? | Humeroulnar | Humeroradial | Proximal radioulnar | Glenohumeral | C | R | Radioulnar pivot | | 21 | Which nerve supplies palmaris longus? | Median | Ulnar | AIN | Radial | A | R | Median nerve | | 22 | Which artery runs on the interosseous membrane? | Radial | Ulnar | AIN artery | PIN artery | C | R | AIN artery | | 23 | Injury to the radial head most likely limits which movement? | Flexion | Pronation and supination | Abduction | Adduction | B | A | Radioulnar movement | | 24 | Supracondylar fracture in a child most likely injures which artery? | Radial | Brachial | Ulnar | Anterior interosseous | B | An | Brachial artery near supracondylar region | | 25 | Which muscle abducts the thumb? | APL | EPB | EPL | EI | A | R | APL | ## B. Essay prompts (with marking guide) E1 (Understand, 10 marks). Describe the boundaries and contents of the cubital fossa and state the clinical relevance of each content. - Marking guide: boundaries 4 marks (medial, lateral, superior, floor). Contents with correct order 3 marks. Clinical relevance 3 marks (venepuncture, brachial pulse). E2 (Analyse, 15 marks). A patient presents with a humeral shaft fracture and wrist drop. Explain the nerve involved, its course, and the motor and sensory deficit. - Marking guide: nerve and root levels 3 marks. Course (spiral groove) 4 marks. Motor deficit (wrist and digit extension) 4 marks. Sensory deficit (dorsal hand) 2 marks. Management 2 marks. E3 (Apply, 10 marks). List the muscles of the anterior forearm by layer and state the nerve supply of each. - Marking guide: 1 mark per correct muscle with nerve (max 10). E4 (Analyse, 15 marks). Compare tennis elbow and golfer's elbow: origin, muscle involved, pain pattern, and exam finding. - Marking guide: origin 3 marks each side, muscle 3, pain pattern 3, test 3. E5 (Evaluate, 10 marks). A surgeon needs to avoid nerve injury during a forearm fasciotomy. Which nerves are at risk in the anterior compartment, and where? - Marking guide: median (at the carpal tunnel and between the heads of pronator teres) 4 marks. AIN (on interosseous membrane) 3 marks. Ulnar (behind medial epicondyle) 3 marks. ## C. Key (objective answers) 1-B, 2-B, 3-C, 4-C, 5-C, 6-B, 7-B, 8-C, 9-A, 10-C, 11-C, 12-A, 13-B, 14-A, 15-A, 16-A, 17-A, 18-B, 19-A, 20-C, 21-A, 22-C, 23-B, 24-B, 25-A.

resources.title: 🧩 4 · Scenarios & Vignettes: Elbow & Forearm — 200L Anatomy
resources.content: > How to use: Read the vignette, decide the answer, then read the reasoning. Bloom levels: A apply, An analyse, E evaluate. | # | Vignette | Question | Answer | Reasoning | Bloom | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | SC1 | A 28-year-old cyclist falls on an outstretched hand and cannot extend his wrist or metacarpophalangeal joints. Sensation over the dorsum of the hand is reduced. | Which nerve and site? | Radial nerve at the spiral groove (or humeral shaft) | Wrist extension and MCP extension are radial innervated; dorsal hand sensory loss is radial superficial branch. | A | | SC2 | A 45-year-old office worker has pain on the lateral elbow when lifting a cup. Pain is worse on resisted wrist extension with the elbow straight. | Which origin is affected? | Common extensor origin at the lateral epicondyle (ECRB most commonly) | Tennis elbow. Resisted wrist extension reproduces pain at the origin. | An | | SC3 | A 60-year-old presents with pain and tingling in the thumb, index and middle finger at night. Thenar wasting is seen. | Which nerve, and where? | Median nerve at the carpal tunnel | Thenar wasting and sensory loss in digits 1–3 = median nerve compression at the wrist. | An | | SC4 | After a forearm laceration, a patient cannot flex the thumb's distal phalanx or the index fingertip (OK sign). There is no sensory loss. | Which nerve, and what is spared? | AIN (motor only). Spared: superficial flexor and sensation. | OK sign loss = AIN. Sensation is normal because AIN is motor only. | A | | SC5 | A child falls on an outstretched arm and has a supracondylar humerus fracture. Pulse is weak in the wrist, hand is pale. | Which vessel is at risk and why? | Brachial artery. Its branches become the radial and ulnar arteries. | Fracture near the brachial artery as it lies anterior to the elbow. Wrist pulse weakness suggests arterial compromise. | E | | SC6 | A 35-year-old has a claw hand (digits 4–5) after elbow injury. He cannot adduct the fingers. | Which nerve and where? | Ulnar nerve, often at the cubital tunnel (behind medial epicondyle) | Claw hand digits 4–5 and loss of adduction = ulnar nerve. Cubital tunnel is the common site. | A | ## Real-life add-on - SC2 links to real life: typing and phone use cause tennis elbow. Advise rest, stretching, and an exercise programme. - SC5 links to real life: the cubital fossa is the standard IV site. Watch for the brachial artery when you insert the needle.

Other sources are named in each row. Verify every row against your Bowen lecturer's notes before exam use. ## A. Glossary (OpenStax key terms, relevant to the forearm) | Term | Definition | Source | | --- | --- | --- | | Anterior compartment of the forearm | (Also anterior flexor compartment) deep and superficial muscles that originate on the humerus and insert into the hand | OpenStax Key Terms | | Deep posterior compartment of the forearm | (Also deep posterior extensor compartment) abductor pollicis longus, extensor pollicis brevis, extensor pollicis longus, extensor indicis, and their associated blood vessels and nerves | OpenStax Key Terms | | Anconeus | Small muscle on the lateral posterior elbow that extends the forearm | OpenStax Key Terms | | Agonist | (Also prime mover) muscle whose contraction is responsible for producing a particular motion | OpenStax Key Terms | | Abduct | Move away from midline in the sagittal plane | OpenStax Key Terms | | Abductor | Moves the bone away from the midline | OpenStax Key Terms | ## B. Objective questions drawn from web and open sources | # | Question | A | B | C | D | Answer | Bloom | Source / note | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | W1 | How many layers does the anterior forearm have? | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | C | R | Superficial, intermediate, deep (AnatomyZone) | | W2 | How many flexor muscles are in the anterior forearm compartment? | 6 | 8 | 10 | 12 | B | R | 5 superficial and 3 deep (novice-medic summary; Wikipedia mirror) | | W3 | How many deep anterior muscles are there? | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | B | R | FDP, FPL, pronator quadratus (JoVE, Kiwix) | | W4 | Repetitive overuse of the forearm extensors most commonly causes which condition? | Golfer's elbow | Tennis elbow | Carpal tunnel | Cubital tunnel | B | A | Lateral epicondylitis (AnatomyZone) | | W5 | Increased pressure within the forearm compartments can cause which problem? | Only bone fracture | Compromised blood flow and nerve function | Joint dislocation | Ligament rupture | B | U | Compartment syndrome (Pearson study guide) | | W6 | How many muscles make up the deep posterior compartment of the forearm? | 2 | 3 | 4 | 6 | C | R | APL, EPB, EPL, EI (JoVE) | | W7 | Which muscle of the posterior compartment is described as lying on the lateral side? | ECRL | Anconeus | ECU | EDM | A | U | ECRL is lateral (Notes section 6) | | W8 | What is the anterior forearm compartment mainly responsible for? | Extension and supination | Flexion and pronation | Abduction | Adduction | B | R | Flexors and pronators (Osmosis/AnatomyZone) | | W9 | What is the posterior forearm compartment mainly responsible for? | Flexion and pronation | Extension and supination | Rotation only | Abduction only | B | R | Extensors and supinators (Osmosis/AnatomyZone) | | W10 | Which nerve innervates most of the posterior compartment? | Median | Ulnar | Radial | Musculocutaneous | C | R | Radial nerve (Osmosis) | ## C. Key W1-C, W2-B, W3-B, W4-B, W5-B, W6-C, W7-A, W8-B, W9-B, W10-C. ## D. Verification list - W2: the count of 8 is consistent across sources. Check the exact count against Bowen's notes. - W10: the posterior compartment is mainly radial. The PIN carries the deep motor branch, so the 'most of' wording matters. - Any source conflict (for example, in how many muscles sit in each superficial group) should be marked here before exam use.
